sections.label: The market landscape
paragraphs: I studied the Danish food delivery market and looked at competitors like HelloFresh and Too Good To Go. I talked with the founders, marketing, and operations about what set Eat Grim apart.

sections.label: Understanding the audience
paragraphs: The people who cared wanted convenience, health, and transparency. Messaging couldn't run on guilt. It had to be something they wanted to join.

sections.label: Visual approach
paragraphs: The brand needed to be playful and bold, with colors that made wonky vegetables look exciting. Illustrations stayed hand-drawn and warm, not corporate.

sections.label: Unboxing experience
paragraphs: Opening a box should feel like more than receiving groceries.

sections.label: Creating consistency
paragraphs: The toolkit held the logo, typeface, color palette, and a recognizable wonky-fruit symbol. People could spot Eat Grim on Instagram, in the mailbox, or on a sticker.

sections.label: Packaging as storytelling
paragraphs: Each box size used bold visuals, short notes, and a friendly tone to say where the food came from and why it mattered.

sections.label: Digital presence
paragraphs: The website made signing up straightforward while explaining why the produce mattered.

sections.label: Visual content
paragraphs: Photography and illustration treated imperfect produce as the hero. Social posts, newsletters, and campaigns paired those images with behind-the-scenes stories.

sections.label: The growth
paragraphs: Eat Grim reached 2,500 regular subscribers during the two-year collaboration. The work got people talking about food waste.

sections.label: Changing perception
paragraphs: The playful, punchy design made sustainability feel exciting instead of guilt-inducing. Bold images and color made the weekly box feel like a good choice.

sections.label: Long-term impact
paragraphs: Curious customers started telling their friends, and they kept choosing Eat Grim.
